core: A boundary/border as a line — and the vertical plane along it — that divides one sovereign territory from another, including the airspace above and subsoil below
How a boundary is made, in sequence: defined (described in a treaty) -> delimited (drawn on a map) -> demarcated (marked on the ground) -> administered (managed and enforced)
Origin typology of boundaries: geometric (straight lines / latitude-longitude), physical/natural (rivers, mountains), and cultural/ethnographic (following language or religion)
Evolution typology relative to settlement: antecedent, subsequent, superimposed, and relict boundaries
The functions of borders: controlling movement of people and goods, and marking identity through inclusion and exclusion
The general typology of boundary DISPUTES: definitional, locational, operational, and allocational — as conceptual categories only
The contrast between a boundary (a line) and a frontier (a zone of transition)
supporting: The distinction between a border/boundary as a precise line and older frontier zones that separated states before fixed lines existed
Non-controversial illustrative examples: the ~49th parallel as a geometric boundary; the Pyrenees and Andes as physical/mountain boundaries; the Great Wall of China as a relict boundary
Irredentism as a general concept arising where boundaries split a cultural group

claims.claim: A boundary is essentially a line, and the vertical plane along that line, that separates one state's territory from another; it includes the airspace above the surface line and the ground (subsoil) below it.

Establishing a boundary proceeds through stages: delimitation is the legal formalization of the boundary in a treaty, with its position plotted on a topographic map and set out in a written description; demarcation is the physical marking of the boundary's course on the ground with boundary markers.

A common four-stage account of boundary-making runs definition (the boundary is described in words in a treaty), delimitation (it is drawn on a map), demarcation (it is marked on the ground), and administration (it is managed and enforced through customs, patrols, and law).

By origin, geographers distinguish physical (natural) boundaries that follow features such as rivers, lakes, and mountains; geometric boundaries that are straight lines, often coinciding with a line of latitude or longitude; and cultural/ethnographic boundaries drawn on a cultural trait such as a shared language or religion.

By their evolution relative to settlement, boundaries are classified as antecedent (drawn before an area was settled), subsequent (drawn after settlement, respecting existing cultural patterns), superimposed (drawn after settlement but ignoring those patterns, often by an outside or conquering power), and relict (no longer functioning as a border but still visible in the landscape). This time-based scheme is associated with Richard Hartshorne.

Almost half of Africa's boundaries are geometric, and at least 177 ethnic groups are split across two or more states; such superimposed, externally drawn lines that cut across cultural patterns are widely associated with later cross-border tension.

Borders function to create zones of inclusion (those inside a territory) and exclusion (those outside it), and they control the movement of people and goods; they are not static but constantly evolving.

Geographers categorize disputes over boundaries into general types: definitional (positional) disputes over the wording and interpretation of the defining treaty or map; locational (territorial) disputes over where the line actually lies or which side territory belongs to; operational (functional) disputes over how the border is managed and how movement across it is regulated; and allocational (resource) disputes over resources that cross or lie beneath the line.

A frontier is a zone rather than a line: historically states were separated by areas, not precise lines, and the intervening zone that limited direct contact between them was called a frontier; a frontier is the geographical area near or beyond a boundary.
Irredentism is an effort by a state to extend its political influence over a group of people in a neighboring state, a tension that can arise where a boundary splits a cultural group.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The names used for the four boundary-dispute categories vary between textbooks.
positions: One common set labels them definitional, locational, operational, and allocational.
An older/alternative set labels them positional, territorial, functional, and resource (transboundary).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Present the four categories by the most widely used names (definitional, locational, operational, allocational) and note the alternative labels, since the underlying categories match: definitional=positional, locational=territorial, operational=functional, allocational=resource.

sourceRecords.title: Introduction to Human Geography (Dorrell & Henderson), 8.4: Boundaries and Boundary Disputes
sourceRecords.provider: Social Sci LibreTexts / University of North Georgia Press (GALILEO)
sourceRecords.notes: Open geography textbook (page tagged license:ccby, licenseversion:40; source@ web.ung.edu/media/university-press/human-geography.pdf). Supports the boundary as an invisible vertical plane including airspace and subsoil; physical boundaries (Rio Grande, Pyrenees, Zagros, Andes); geometric boundaries along latitude/longitude (49 deg N US-Canada; 141st meridian Indonesia-Papua New Guinea); ethnic boundaries drawn on language/religion; irredentism; and the figures that almost 50% of Africa's boundaries are geometric with at least 177 ethnic groups split across states. Facts adapted and reworded; no long excerpts reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: The Eastern World: Daily Readings on Geography — Political Geography I: Borders
sourceRecords.provider: College of DuPage (Joel Quam & Scott Campbell), via Pressbooks
sourceRecords.notes: Open text used as reference (NonCommercial/ShareAlike license, so no prose reproduced). Attributes the origin-based classification (physiographic, anthropogeographic, geometric) to Samuel W. Boggs and the time-based classification (pioneer/antecedent, subsequent, superimposed, relict) to Richard Hartshorne, and notes the two schemes combine (e.g., a superimposed boundary can also be geometric). The Great Wall of China is given as an anthropogeographic/relict-type example. Used for the two typologies; all illustrative real-world disputes in the source were deliberately NOT used, per the no-side-taking rule.

sourceRecords.title: The Eastern World: Daily Readings on Geography — Political Geography II: Border Disputes
sourceRecords.provider: College of DuPage (Joel Quam & Scott Campbell), via Pressbooks
sourceRecords.notes: Companion chapter categorizing border disputes into four general kinds: positional (over documentation/treaty wording), territorial (over which side holds the land, incl. historical claims), functional (over policy/land-use practices at the border, e.g. passports and visas), and transboundary resource (over resources crossing the line). These map to the widely used AP/political-geography names definitional, locational, operational, and allocational. Used ONLY for the abstract typology; the source's specific disputed cases were not reproduced and no position was taken on any of them.

sourceRecords.title: Delimitation and Demarcation of State Boundaries (handbook)
sourceRecords.provider: Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE)
sourceRecords.notes: Intergovernmental handbook. Defines a state boundary as 'a line and the vertical plane going along the line, determining the limits of a state's territory (its land, waters, subsoil and airspace)'; delimitation of the boundary as its legal formalization in a treaty, with position plotted on a topographic map and set out in a written description; and demarcation as marking out the boundary's course on the ground with boundary markers plus demarcation documents. Read as a PDF via the OSCE CDN copy; used as reference for the vertical-plane definition and the delimitation/demarcation stages, prose written originally.

sourceRecords.title: Boundary (encyclopedic entry)
sourceRecords.notes: Plain-language reference defining a boundary as 'a real or imaginary line that separates two things,' and distinguishing physical boundaries (rivers, mountain ranges, oceans, deserts), political boundaries (created by people to separate areas governed by different groups, usually invisible), and cultural/linguistic boundaries. Used as reference for the definition and the physical/political/cultural split; prose written originally.

sourceRecords.title: Border (encyclopedic entry)
sourceRecords.notes: Reference defining a border as 'a physical or political line that separates geographic areas,' outlining the area a particular governing body controls, and used to delineate countries, states, provinces, counties, and cities. Used as reference for the border definition and the control-of-territory function; prose written originally.

sourceRecords.title: GEOG 571, 4.3: Borders and Boundaries Defined
sourceRecords.provider: Penn State College of Earth and Mineral Sciences
sourceRecords.notes: University course material framing borders as more than a simple line: as political limits and assertions of power over space, creating zones of 'inclusion' and 'exclusion,' and constantly evolving rather than static. Used as reference for the functions of borders; prose written originally.

sourceRecords.title: Boundary and Frontiers (lecture note)
sourceRecords.notes: Academic lecture note stating the classical distinction: in the past states were separated by areas, not lines, and the intervening zone that prevented direct contact was called a frontier; a frontier is the political and geographical area near or beyond a boundary, whereas a boundary is a line clearly identified by treaty. Used as a supporting reference for the boundary-line vs frontier-zone contrast, a non-controversial classical concept; prose written originally.
